source.title: Learning Rate Matters: Vanilla LoRA May Suffice for LLM Fine-tuning
source.authors: Yu-Ang Lee; Ching-Yun Ko; Pin-Yu Chen; M. Yeh

record.file_problem: Whole paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Tests batch-size effects on held-out performance in LLM fine-tuning, extending the large-batch question to decoder-only language models with learning rates tuned.
record.gate_note: The study reports held-out task accuracy and Hessian eigenvalues, but not training error or a train-test generalization gap. Its results on batch size bear on V5; Hessian results concern optimal learning rates, not whether a measured property tracks the generalization gap. Results cited from other work are not cataloged as rows.
record.test_reason: The study tests V5 in a new setting: parameter-efficient fine-tuning of decoder-only language models. Batch-size comparisons hold training at one epoch and measure held-out accuracy, with learning rates tuned separately. Training error or a train-test gap is not required to test V5's held-out-performance claim.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate: learning-rate tuning largely removes systematic peak-performance advantages of the tested LoRA variants, although modest rank-dependent differences remain. The authors recommend prioritizing learning-rate tuning and using small or medium batches because very large batches can reduce attainable accuracy.
record.recipe_differences: LLM parameter-efficient fine-tuning with AdamW, not the original studies' image-classifier or language-model training recipes. Learning rate was tuned; batch size was varied in selected experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Batch size changes best-achievable performance at B ≥ 256 in the tested Gemma-3-1B setting. The paper also reports method-specific learning-rate ranges and rank-dependent performance patterns, but these do not measure the claim versions' train-test gap.

fits_no_version.finding: Initial block-wise Hessian eigenvalues differ among LoRA initialization methods and help explain their preferred learning-rate ranges.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Initial loss curvature predicts relative effective learning-rate ranges for LoRA methods.

fits_no_version.finding: LoRA and its variants generally attain comparable peak benchmark performance after method-specific learning-rate tuning.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Apparent performance advantages among LoRA variants often disappear after learning-rate tuning.

record.problems: The study reports test-task accuracy rather than train error or a train-test gap. The large-batch evidence is for one model, one task, two methods and one rank; the exact values at B ≥ 256 are figure-only. The paper states that many secondary settings were fixed and that hyperparameter search was not exhaustive.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows for the batch-size result are required: the main text gives aggregate text for B ≤ 128 and describes decay for B ≥ 256, while Figure 11 provides separate values only graphically. Other tables vary learning rate and report task accuracy for many method-batch combinations, but they do not report train-test gaps and do not add distinct evidence beyond the batch-size finding cataloged here.

untested.parts: Random-label fitting and its coexistence with natural-label generalization.
Network widening beyond zero training error. Adapter-rank sweeps do not establish this condition.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers and local-connectivity explanations.
Adaptive optimizers versus SGD or momentum SGD. Comparisons among LoRA methods using AdamW do not test this version.
Image classifiers; whether longer training closes a large-batch penalty; interventions on warmup, normalization, or regularization. Duration sweeps at batch 64 do not test recovery at large batches.
Dropout interventions. Dropout and weight decay are both absent throughout the relevant experiments.
Magnitude-aware perturbation tolerance, its correlation with train-test gaps, and comparison with norm- or margin-based measures.
Identifying memorized examples, removing them, and comparing retraining with random removal.

missing.what: A direct learning-rate adaptation comparison: at fixed learning rate 2e-4, LoRA accuracy falls from 20.00±0.26% at batch 16 to 15.92±0.45% at batch 128; tuning the latter to 1.1e-3 yields 20.32±0.28%. The record mentions excluding other tables but overlooks this distinct evidence for V5's recipe-adaptation clause.
missing.locator: Section 3.3.1, Table 1; repeated in Appendix Table 8

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for these versions. Table 5 establishes a fixed one-epoch budget, correcting the record's claim that fixed-epoch comparisons were not tested. Similar performance at batches 16–128 is consistent with V5's workload-dependent threshold and does not challenge it. Exact accuracies at batches 256 and 512 are unavailable in the supplied text; the authors' explicit description supports the direction of their effect.

versions.untested_parts: Random-label memorization and natural-label held-out generalization.
Width sweeps of one-hidden-layer ReLU networks past the interpolation threshold.
Convolutional versus fully connected image classifiers.
Comparisons of adaptive optimizers with SGD or momentum SGD.

The study tests batch size in decoder-only LLM fine-tuning with learning-rate tuning. It does not test image classifiers, fixed-epoch comparisons against smaller batches under an untuned recipe, or the listed remedies involving longer training, warmup, normalization, or regularization changes.
Effects of adding or removing dropout and weight decay on held-out error.
Whether magnitude-aware perturbation sharpness tracks train-test gaps; the paper measures Hessian curvature in relation to optimal learning-rate ranges.
Removing and retraining after memorized examples are identified.

rows.note: The prose reports this aggregate across batch sizes B ≤ 128, rather than separate exact values for each batch.
rows.check: Approximately constant tuned accuracy across the tested batches 16–128 indicates no batch-size penalty in this range; 20% accuracy alone is not an observed penalty. Specify the one-epoch budget and mean GSM8K/MATH accuracy after training on 100k MetaMathQA examples. LoRA is an adaptation method, not the model.
